utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom and those assisting us just outside the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we invite the Defence to call its next witness, there are a few practical matters on our agenda, the first one being that the Defence has asked some time in relation to what I would call the Savkic exhibits. We would like to address the issue of these exhibits relating to Witness Savkic, and we are talking about P1055, 1056, 1057, 1059, 1060, 1065, and 1066. On the 2nd of March, the Chamber requested the Defence to either file a brief written submission or to address the matter in court, and I hear now Mr. Josse will need five minutes. Since we did not receive any submissions, we now give you an opportunity to respond to the Prosecution on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that I do that tomorrow. I've consulted -- or Mr. Stewart has consulted with our learned friends from the Prosecution. This is all to do with the various timetabling difficulties that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there is -- there are a few other matters on which I'll give you -- not always a decision but sometimes a statement, and I'll start with a statement of guidance requested by the Defence. In a motion of the 2nd of March, 2006, the Defence has asked that the Chamber could assist a Defence witness in obtaining a passport. The Chamber is aware that it is unusual for the Tribunal to request passports from local authorities, in particular because this might draw undue attention to those persons as prospective witnesses. However, should the Defence have a specific, different request, the Chamber is ready to hear it. But -- and there's no difference of treatment between Defence and Prosecution witnesses in this respect. The Defence has also approached the Chamber with a request for guidance regarding the addition of new witnesses to its list, and the Chamber allows this modification to the list of witnesses on the understanding that the time limits for the Defence case remain the same. Then the next issue I would like to address is -- I'd like to address the Defence regarding the potential testimony of the accused. If the accused decides to give oral evidence, the Chamber notes that, according to the Rule 65 ter summary provided, the Defence intends to address the topic of the accused's personal history during the examination of this witness. In order to make the most efficient use of his testimony pursuant to Rule 89(F) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Chamber invites the Defence to make a written submission on this topic. The submission could include, but need not to be limited to: Family, education and training, places of residence, personal interests, and early professional career. The Chamber suggests that the submission not address the accused's professional career related to the indictment. The Defence is also invited to include a description of the circumstances of the accused's arrest in April 2000. And for the purposes of this submission, the Defence may include information on the accused's personal history, both before and after the indictment period. The Chamber would like to emphasise that the submission does not preclude examination on these topics by either party and Judges. The Chamber asks that the submission be filed two weeks prior to the commencement of the accused's testimony. I now would like to address the Defence regarding its e-mail message dated the 2nd March, 2006, in which it expressed its preference for the Chamber to recess on Friday, the 21st, and Monday, the 24th of April, 2006, in observance of Orthodox Easter. The Chamber is sympathetic to the religious practices of the accused, witnesses, and Tribunal staff. Under the circumstances, however, the Chamber is unable to follow the Defence's suggestion. The current schedule of this case leaves the Chamber no flexibility to choose the days on which it will sit. In addition, the Chamber is required to respect UN holidays, and thus cannot sit on those days due to the unavailability of support staff. Two additional days of recess would make it more difficult for the Chamber to hear as much of the most highly relevant evidence as possible in the time frame allotted for the case. However, since the courtroom schedule has not yet been determined for the month of April, the Chamber is willing to explore with other Chambers and the Registry the possibility of sitting for a morning session on Friday, the 21st of April, and an afternoon session on Monday, the 24th of April, in order to allow the accused the maximum amount of uninterrupted time for religious observance. And the Chamber asks that the Defence inform the Chamber at this time if it would like the Chamber to make such a request. The Trial Chamber would like to address the Prosecution and the Defence regarding source material and photographic material. The Chamber has sought access to material on other occasions to assist it in the understanding and evaluation of the evidence presented. It has done so in respect of Prosecution witnesses and Defence witnesses. For example, the Chamber sought additional information on the death of Husein Hotic, referred to by Witness Pasic, in December 2005, as well as the production of Witness Prstojevic's diaries in June 2005. With respect to the source material, paragraphs 337 through 349 of the Nielsen report discuss the Republika Srpska MUP draft annual report for 1992, produced by the Republika Srpska Ministry of Internal affairs in January of 1993. Paragraph 347 makes reference to: "An abundance of internal and external reports related to internal affairs and the security situation which had been produced," including approximately 150 issues of the "Bulletin of Daily Events," over 90 documents received by the Prime Minister, and over 80 documents received by the president and members of the Presidency. Dr. Nielsen testified, based on his analysis, that the reports to high-level officials contained no reference to women and children being rounded up in mopping-up operations and that the daily bulletins from 1992 contain "very little trace" of references to detention facilities and mopping-up operations. This testimony is on transcript pages 13945 to 13955 -- I made a mistake. I said -- I think I said "45" but I repeat it: The testimony is on transcript pages on pages 13954 to 13955. The Chamber finds it probable that the source material Dr. Nielsen relied upon would enable the Chamber to better understand the reporting mechanisms he describes. It may also provide the Chamber with a more objective basis to verify his conclusions. The Chamber would therefore like to ask whether the following groups of documents are available to the Prosecution, in order of preference, if this matter requires further research: First, the group of over 80 documents received by the president and members of the Presidency; second, the group of over 90 documents received by the Prime Minister; and third, the group of approximately 150 issues of the Bulletin of Daily Events. The Prosecution may reply orally as soon as I have finished reading this statement or by e-mail to the Chamber's staff by the end of business on Friday, the 10th of March, 2006. The Chamber would also like to request from the parties photographic material regarding the destruction of property. During both the Prosecution and the Defence cases, the Chamber has been presented with evidence on the destruction of property during and following the attacks and take-over of towns, villages, and municipalities. This evidence has included witness testimony, various forms of documentation, and some photographic material, notably photographs submitted by an expert witness on destruction of cultural property. Evidence has been presented, both in respect of indictment municipalities - that evidence was usually led by the Prosecution - and non-indictment municipalities, which was usually led by the Defence. The Chamber finds that oral testimony is often better understood if it is illustrated through pictures. If a witness testified that houses in his village were destroyed, the Chamber would like to gain a visual impression of such destruction and requests the parties to provide exemplary photographic material from 1992 which illustrates the destruction of property addressed in the presentation of evidence. In relation to the indictment municipalities, the Chamber requests the Prosecution to provide a representative sample, which is not the same as a complete set of. So we are requesting the Prosecution to provide a representative sample of photographic material categorised by municipality, clearly labelling the object of the photograph and the date in 1992 when the photograph was taken. The Defence is also invited to present samples of photographic material for indictment municipalities as well as photographic material for non-indictment municipalities to the extent -- the letter, to the extent addressed in the evidence. However, whereas we are obliging the Prosecution to produce photographs in its possession, the Defence need only submit such material if it wishes to do so. The Chamber requests the parties to submit this material in court no later than the 31st of March. The last matter I'd like to raise is that the Chamber would like to address the Defence regarding video footage related to an attack on a JNA convoy in Tuzla on the 15th of May, 1992. This video footage was referred to by Witness Momcilo Micic on the 13th of December, 2005, and the Defence asked - I refer to transcript page 19455 - whether the Prosecution had disclosed the relevant material to the Defence. At the housekeeping session on the 23rd of February of this year - the transcript page 20846 - the Prosecution confirmed that the videos were in its possession, and on the 28th of February responded to the Chamber that all of the requested material had been delivered to the Defence. The Chamber is now inquiring whether the Defence has had the opportunity to review this material; and, if so, whether it intends to introduce it as evidence. These were the matters the Chamber wanted to raise at this moment prior to inviting the Defence to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, may I specifically draw the attention of the Defence to my invitation to inform us, if possible now, whether the Chamber should make an effort, because that always takes some time and the earlier you are, the better the chances are, to try to schedule sitting on Friday, the 21st of April, in the morning - and we all know that the Friday afternoon is not the most popular moment to sit - and to sit on Monday, the 24th of April in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Most certainly, Your Honour. There are three or four points that Your Honour raises that I can very quickly deal with. The first on that -- well, thank you for the offer, Your Honours, but it's apparent through communication here that that particular change is a matter of relative indifference to Mr. Krajisnik, in which case we wouldn't ask the Trial Chamber or anybody else to go to any trouble in relation to that particular issue. But thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I hope it's clear enough that the Chamber is not in any way in control on whether the UN observes Orthodox Easter or any other Easter available. So therefore, we have to follow. Otherwise -- if choices would have been made otherwise, we would have followed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did explain to Mr. Krajisnik that such decisions were taken at a different level in different circumstances. We understand that. Second, Your Honour, in relation to what we do understand - and thank you again - is the Chamber's readiness to assist if it can in relation to the passport. We hope that isn't going to arise, Your Honour. We're going to pursue that again this evening to see what the up-to-date position is. But thank you, Your Honour. If there is something specific, we will, with respect, come back to the Trial Chamber straight away on that. So far as the video footage is concerned, Your Honour, that has been viewed by a member of our team, obviously one of our B/C/S speakers. I will need to speak to him about it, Your Honour. I think the next point is -- yes, in relation to the suggestion, as a part of Mr. Krajisnik prospective testimony that might dealt with by 89(F), I'm happy to tell Your Honour that what Your Honour has indicated matches just about a hundred per cent what is in advanced preparation, so there should be absolutely no difficulty in meeting that timetable and, with respect, we concur that that is a more than sensible way of dealing with that particular aspect of the evidence. Your Honour, I think those are all the practical points on which an immediate response might be helpful from me right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll see for the 21st and the 24th of April, you say it's not very substantial, then the Chamber will feel free to follow any other wish expressed by parties or preferences expressed within the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Perhaps there's one more thing I should say, Your Honour, since we have had some disruption, just absolutely briefly, just really to put on the record so that people understand what's happened. The witness that was going to come was, first of all, affected by the very bad weather in southern Europe and then very unhappily when that witness finally was either at or very near to the airport was then suddenly and unexpectedly affected by a particular personal situation which meant that he was unable to travel, and it was unreasonable to ask him to travel in those circumstances, so that double -- those double incidents, Your Honour, have put us in the unfortunate position of not having that witness. It's regrettable, but it was not under anybody's control in the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've asked myself whether, due to the very tight schedule we have at this moment, whether such a late arrival of witnesses -- and of course these personal circumstances would not have been influenced by it, but of course snow doesn't fall every day, whether we would always work as close to the edge, with all the risks of falling off. So therefore, if the Defence would try to get a little bit more time on arrival of witnesses. I do not know exactly what the rules are, how much time there would be available for the Defence to invite the witnesses to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I absolutely assure Your Honour that as a matter of fact the Defence, we always do what we can to bring the witnesses as early as possible, but the limitations imposed, first of all, quite naturally, Your Honour, by -- negotiation with a witness as to how much time they spend away from home is number one; and secondly, we always have, in effect, to negotiate it - and they are very helpful - with the Victims and Witnesses Section, so, Your Honour, we certainly follow the policy of bringing witnesses here as early as possible. And I indicated specifically to the Trial Chamber yesterday that in relation to the next witnesses coming up, I specifically made the choice and made the request and gave instructions, as necessary, to bring this witness earlier rather than later, which has had exactly the beneficial effect that Your Honour indicates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to stress that if there are any bureaucratic reasons which would prevent you from getting the witnesses here at such time that not every minor delay would create an empty courtroom and no hearing of evidence, that the Chamber certainly would assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that -- certainly, Your Honour. We take account weather, but it's a bit difficult when the weather is worse than since records began in parts of southern Europe and we can't really anticipate that. But, Your Honour, we note the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, we've heard from Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I was just -- Mr. Josse just wanted to consult on something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I wanted to address -- I -- unless there's anything else you would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I think -- while consulting with Mr. Josse, I heard my name and sometimes if I hear my name, in a Pavlovian way, Your Honour, I just stand -- I just get on my feet, but I'll reverse the Pavlovian process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's not easy because it's a Pavlovian process. Mr. Harmon, you were invited to -- or at least I said you may reply orally as to the availability of the documents referred to on the Nielsen report, but you have an opportunity to give us the information through e-mail to our staff by the end of business on next Friday. I don't know which one you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have made an inquire by e-mail to see if those documents are available. Perhaps I can give you an oral response today by the close of business; and if not, I will respond by e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll keep that in mind. Having dealt with the practical issues, we are now at a point that the Chamber invites the Defence to call its next witness. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, I'm going to ask for a short period of time. It really fits in with the issue to do with the witness who couldn't get here. Clearly my personal and our team preparations have been badly affected by the situation. I had some e-mail contact with Mr. Harmon yesterday. Mr. Stewart spoke to him. The Prosecution have understandably informed the Defence that they will be unable to cross-examine this witness today in any event. Could I ask for a break now of 40 minutes. The witness is in the building. I promised him I would see him once again, and then I will commence my examination of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you consider it to be a possibility to finish his examination-in-chief today?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think there's a -- I think there's a -- a chance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's then take that break immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 40 minutes' adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, just on that single point about the video, the answer is: Yes, Your Honour, we do propose to adduce that video in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I take it, Mr. Harmon, there's no need to have this video introduced through any witness or it's -- could just be -- you would not oppose --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then, Mr. Stewart, if you would tender it, it will then get a number, and as soon as you're ready to do that, the Chamber will admit it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, are you ready to call your next witness, which as I understand would be Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you for the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From your answer, the "dobro jutro," I take it that you can understand me -- that you hear me in a language you understand, Mr. Poplasen. At least, I assume that you're Mr. Poplasen. Mr. Poplasen, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Poplasen. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, you'll be first examined by Mr. Josse, counsel for the Defence. Mr. Josse, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your name is Nikola Poplasen. You graduated in political science at the faculty in the University of Sarajevo in 1969. You then undertook various post-graduate studies, which led eventually to your getting a Ph.D. You then became an academic in the faculty of political science in Sarajevo, and you have published a number of books. That's all correct as a very brief resume of your activities before the war?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes, except for the fact that it wasn't 1969. It was 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. And after the war, you continued as an academic but in Banja Luka. That's also right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: And during the war, from 1993 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We -- your evidence will, for the most part, deal, of course, with your political activities before and during the war, so I will leave those out for a moment. But it is correct, isn't it, that after the war you became, in 1998, the president of the Republika Srpska until you were removed from that office by the then High Representative?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: At the elections in 1998, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were elected in a ballot as president?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were originally a member of the League of Communists. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is right that virtually all political science academics were members of that league?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: A large number of people, all who are of age, according to my analyses, 11 million inhabitants of the former Yugoslavia were at one time or another in the League of Communists. 11 million different people, that was a specific situation in the socialist country where, if one wanted to get any kind of job or promotion, most often they would have to become a member of that league.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Some time prior to the 1990 elections, you left the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: A few years before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were not a candidate in the 1990 elections. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I was not a member of any political party, nor did I participate as a candidate in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As we will learn, you have never been a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No. No, I have never been a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This Chamber has heard evidence from a number of witnesses about fears and concerns of Serbs after the election and in the lead-up to the war. I'm not going to ask you to deal with those topics, but it is right that in 1991 you were invited to join the Political Council of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes. The social and psychological situation for a few years leading up to 1988 and 1989 became very tense in the former Yugoslavia. Tension could be felt between very different social groups, especially ethnic and religious groups. And in the late 1980s, on the political scene of the former Yugoslavia, the so-called national parties grew very strong. In the Republic of Croatia, the Serbian Democratic Party was established first. After that, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Party of Democratic Action was established, advocating mainly Muslim interests; the HDZ advocating Croatian interests; and after that, as a response to all that, the Serb Democratic Party. This party became very popular. It had some very clear national ideas. It participated in the elections in 1990 and obtained the vast majority of Serb votes. It started its activities and established an advisory body which was initially called the Council of the Serb Democratic Party, but later on, when some other auxiliary bodies were established by that party for economics, culture, and so on, the council was no longer an all-purpose council, but was dubbed the Political Advisory Council. The president of this council was for a time Professor Nikola Koljevic, who is a personal acquaintance and friend of mine and had been for many years before those events, and he asked me to become a member of the council, not a member of the SDS, and to participate in the work of that council where I could express my opinions and comments freely, thus contributing to the work of that body. I accepted his invitation, and towards the end of the first half of 1991 I was appointed a member of that council and participated in its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have helpfully dealt there with the advent of the SDS. Did you view the SDS as a regular - by that I mean ordinary - political party, or did you in some way see it in other terms?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I have to first state some general facts which may be of assistance to the Chamber in connection with your question. As regards my personal convictions and view of the events in the late 1980s, it was clear to me that throughout Yugoslavia dramatic events were forthcoming and that within Yugoslavia, but also abroad, there would be forces contributing to the destruction and break-up of that country. The energy of the people was channeled into the national parties. Other forms of association were completely suppressed in the media, in the public speeches of the representatives of the international community, in the public speeches of the newly emerging political elite. And all this was indicating that there would be a renewal of interethnic conflicts. On the other side was a significant group of politicians who had been members of the League of Communists and who were very dogmatic. They were hard-liners, adhering to the conviction that the former Yugoslavia could be preserved. These dogmatic hard-liners relied on some tenets of international law, on the fact that Yugoslavia existed as the only internationally recognised state in the area, and that this Yugoslavia had a very strong army. However, the role of the army was to preserve the external borders. That's what was stated in the constitution of the former Yugoslavia. But they had not counted on the fact that the civilian leadership of Yugoslavia and of the republics of which Yugoslavia consisted - Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Macedonia, and so on - the desire emerged to destroy the then-Yugoslavia. The civilian leaders of Yugoslavia and of the republics, in this case the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were actually looking for other solutions, which would lead to a reorganisation in political terms of the territory making up Yugoslavia. And they were motivated by national ideas. Significant problems arose due to that. This meant that territories with a majority population of a single ethnic group would not experience war, but that it was very likely that a war would break out where the population was mixed. In my view, the Serbs -- when I say "the Serbs," I am referring primarily to the Serb political leaderships but also to the Serb population which had to be educated by the political and cultural elite -- in those circumstances, my expectations were that the Serbs would formulate their own interests in that country which was called Yugoslavia in such a way that everything would be done to avoid bloodshed and to avoid a head-on conflict with members of other national groups and religious affiliations, because the Serbs, for the most part, were Orthodox. Therefore, in my view, there had to be a certain kind of reconstruction of Yugoslavia but with the agreement among the elites of all the nations inhabiting the territory of the former Yugoslavia. SDS formulated, in part, some of my views. The SDS was offensive in its representation of itself to the public and to the members of the other ethnic and national groups. They wanted to find ways, new ways, of living together in which no nation would be subjugated or suppressed in economic, cultural or religious terms. I liked this approach where changes, which were inevitable, were to be expected but where a policy would be followed which would avoid bloodshed and destruction and where compromises would be made in the search for equality. This was the idea advocated by the SDS, and in the Political Council we had many discussions on how Bosnia and Herzegovina could be organised and how the Serb people could be organised. You asked me about the year 1991. One has to understand that Yugoslavia still existed in 1991, and I was aware of the fact that discussions about the Serb people and the -- and Serb interests implied the Serb nation as a whole, all the Serbs living in the former Yugoslavia. This interest had to be brought into dialogue with interests of the other nations; Muslims, Montenegrins, Croats, and so on. This was the key reason for my participating in the work of the Political Council of the SDS. I was not an SDS member, so I was not bound by any statutory norms of the SDS. I was not obliged, as a non-party member, to respect any kind of party discipline. To be sure, I expressed my opinions in public or, on more than one occasion, through the electronic media or through comments in a newspaper called Javnost and other publications in Serbia, Montenegro, and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't stop the witness because, for the most part, he clearly realised that these were all topics that I was going to -- and he's covered many of the issues that I was going to ask him about in subsequent questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, you've gone all -- most of the way, but perhaps not all the way, in explaining exactly why you didn't join the SDS in, shall we say, 1991. I'd like you to explain your thinking in that year, not with the benefit of hindsight; in other words, not -- ignore what happened subsequently. Why in 1991 did you say to yourself: I'm not going to join the SDS?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I apologise, but I don't see the logic behind your question. Activity or public activity, as a member of a political party, is only possible if you have prospects for the future, if you have a goal, something you want to achieve. And this goal is always situated in the future, and it is from this aspect that specific issues are analysed. A man has to decide whether joining a party will lead to the goal he envisages. It was my opinion in that period that the Serbs, as a whole, had to have a goal, which was to live peacefully, without conflicts with other nations or social groups; and in order to achieve this, they had to be connected with each other. The former Yugoslavia gave that, not only to the Serbs but also to the other nations because the Muslims are also scattered in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, Serbia. So are the Albanians, so are the Croats. The Slovenes least of all, that's true. But I was simply weighing whether the Serb Democratic Party would satisfy this orientation of mine. However, as time went on, 1991, 1992, and so on, it became evident that the SDS was wavering; accepting something, then not accepting it. For a time they wanted all the Serbs to live in one state, then they didn't want that. And then the SDS would accept the illegal recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an internationally recognised state. A number of facts emerged where the SDS or its leadership accepted legal violence over the former Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and then based its policies on unacceptable foundations. However, of all the political parties, it most fully advocated the interests of the Serbian people, and that was why I was willing to cooperate and provide support on certain issues but not always. And I did not want to become a member, which would imply that I fully accepted the platform and the statute of the SDS. I was not completely satisfied with the Serbian Democratic Party, although of all the major parties, I found it more congenial than any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Political Council, you've already told us that you and others engaged there in theoretical-type discussions. Was that primarily what its role was, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Well, better to say theoretical political discussions. That was the role of the council in the SDS. The SDS had other bodies making decisions. The Political Council could not make any decisions. There was the Presidency of the SDS, there was the Executive Board, there was the party president. It was up to them, first of all, whether they would attend sessions of the council at all; and secondly, whether they would or would not adopt a suggestion made by the council. It was up to the leadership of the SDS to decide that. The leadership of the SDS was not bound to report to us at all. It was, however, the custom when someone from the leadership attended a session of the Political Council and we had questions, to answer our questions and make some comments to help us in our work. But we were not given any feedback as to what was done with our advice and our suggestions later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, if you would allow me one question for clarification. You said -- when you discussed SDS policy, you said: The SDS would accept the illegal recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an internationally recognised state. Could you give me the factual basis of this statement. When did the SDS express that it would accept the illegal recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an internationally recognised state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, Bosnia and Herzegovina asked for international recognition, but this was contrary to the constitution, without the agreement of the Serbian people and representatives the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand what you meant by "illegal recognition." You said the SDS would accept that illegal recognition. When and where did they accept that and by what means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the recognition, the representatives of the SDS and the members of the state leadership who were SDS members set out to negotiate with the representatives of the Muslim and Croatian people and the international community based on the recognition of the country --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I -- you are referring to the -- what is often called the Cutileiro negotiations? Is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SDS accepted the Cutileiro plan. It accepted it, as did Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and the members of the Muslim people, but he withdrew his signature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, I'm just seeking where you said "the SDS accepted the illegal recognition," what you were referring to. Do I understand that you are referring to the position the SDS and its leadership took in the negotiations which led to the Cutileiro plan? This Chamber has heard evidence on who signed it and who withdrew, and we have heard a lot of evidence. Were you referring to that negotiations when you said "the SDS accepted the illegal recognition of the Bosnia and Herzegovina as an internationally recognised state"? Were you referring to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, after the Cutileiro plan. Your question also included the behaviour of the SDS. It was evident from the behaviour of the SDS that the rejection of the Cutileiro plan, which, in my view, was a good plan for all the nations, that this was leading to a bad situation. And from the behaviour of the SDS, it was evident that this political fact was accepted. They entered into negotiations. To be sure, it was in an attempt to find a new solution and to change something, but they entered the whole procedure of political and legal negotiations, which showed that they were recognising the situation, that they were giving up the idea of a firmer association with other Serb areas. So this was a deviation from the position that the SDS had had before the Cutileiro plan. I don't recall that there was any formal session of any body of the party in which it was stated that they accepted Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it is quite evident from the way they acted that they were accepting this unequally constituted Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still have some problems in understanding this. From the evidence we heard, it seems to appear that once the Cutileiro plan failed, that one of the major developments on from that moment was to -- to have Republika Srpska as the main orientation of the SDS in terms of administration of government -- well, all kind of other matters. I'm just trying to find where you find the -- because it's all rather vague. You say: The behaviour shows that. This Chamber has heard quite some evidence which seems to demonstrate that the main efforts were to have Republika Srpska as the -- as the -- if not state, at least the entity which would take its own decisions on matters relating to government, justice, defence. So therefore, I'm wondering where exactly you saw the behaviour of the SDS to be such that it would still consider the Bosnia and Herzegovina as an accepted, internationally recognised state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will simplify this. The majority of the Serbian people supported the SDS in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was also the SDS in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina within the Republic of Croatia. There was the SDS in Serbia as well, which wasn't as influential and as significant. However, the SDS of Bosnia and Herzegovina was greatly supported by the people in Serbia, even those who were not SDS members in Serbia. What had to be done was the following: The SDS had to lobby strongly for a sort of a meeting, a congress, where the Serbian representatives from all the areas of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which was called at the time the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from Montenegro and Serbia would meet and try to find some sort of an agreement. And this is what the SDS gave up as an idea; that is what I was referring to. I fully agree with your observation that the Serbian Democratic Party was working on making the Republika Srpska stronger in political, economic, and military terms, but it did not work on getting closer to the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, to Serbia, or Montenegro because this problem could only be solved in one way, and this was the main point of contention of a difference in position between the SDS and the Serbian Radical Party. I concluded from there that the SDS leadership --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please -- please finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, based on this fact that I mentioned, I concluded that the political moves and the conduct of the SDS were focussed on Bosnia-Herzegovina as an internationally recognised state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I well understand your testimony, you say: While giving up the perspective of being united in one state, all Serbs being united in one state, that, for you, made clear that the SDS was accepting Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, roughly, that is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was asking you about the Political Council. You had - and again helpfully - made some reference to the leadership of the SDS and their involvement in that council. Perhaps before we turn to that, it's right that you attended approximately 50 per cent of the meetings of the Political Council whilst you were a member of that body?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Probably yes, although I did not keep minutes or have notes of that. I suppose that I attended roughly 50 per cent - not less - of the meetings. The council met once weekly, rather frequently, therefore. I was not able to attend some of them, but I attended others.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The leadership attended intermittently. Could I ask you first about Radovan Karadzic. How frequently did he attend, if you're able to say?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: One could not say that he attended the meetings on a regular basis. He attended the meetings periodically, probably when his duties permitted him to do so. Radovan Karadzic also attended periodically, Professor Koljevic chaired the meetings, Mrs. Plavsic also attended the meetings. Mr. Krajisnik attended several of these meetings, I don't know how many as well, and probably some other members of the Executive Board. I did not pay particular attention to that and to see who was there in terms of their role; I was more focussed on the discussion of those who attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on the contributions, if any, made by Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: He did not take, really, an active part in the meetings. He followed the discussion. He did not raise any issues in particular. I only recall his reaction to our statement that something was happening, he would merely say that the party leadership was taking care of those matters. He did not clarify what he meant by that. His interventions were rather brief and mostly had to do with the fact that he had been informed of a matter or with -- with providing some information. He would tell us that the party leadership had taken appropriate decisions. Perhaps he did not trust the Political Council that much because the council consisted of some people who were not members of the SDS. He was, perhaps for that particular reason, very brief in his addresses and did not go into any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Same question, please, for Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Mr. Krajisnik attended these meetings several times, and I recall him just as I see him now. He normally took notes during the meetings. In the intervals to these meetings, since he was already at the time the speaker of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the Assembly or, in particular, after the close of these meetings, I recall that at the time the parliamentary sessions were broadcast live on the TV and I had several questions to put to him on some occasions. He answered that it was very difficult to secure the equality of all the peoples and that we had to be aware of the fact that we were just one of the peoples there, that all of his efforts were focussed on this, but that he would never lose the Serb interests out of sight. I took him to be a busy sort of man; that's why I did not pursue him with any questions. I was not a personal acquaintance of Mr. Krajisnik, and that is why I did not meet with him outside these council meetings. This exchange of ours that we had would take place either during the breaks or after these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to clarify that. You didn't know Mr. Krajisnik before 1991. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I can't be very specific, but I definitely did not know him before 1990. It is possible that in the course of 1990 I met him because I used to take a walk and talk to Mr. Koljevic, and then we would go to the office of the SDS Main Board, where we would meet the members of the board. And I might have met with Mr. Krajisnik there, although I'm not sure, of course. In the past several years I met hundreds of people and I tend to forget the dates and the names. In any case, we did not meet before 1990. In 1991, through the Political Council, and in particular through Mr. Krajisnik's political activity, his personality could be outlined. I don't think he could have had any impression as to my personality because I was not that public a person. However, I grew to know him in that period, especially with the start of the war operations, when we met and socialised more frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, may I ask for one clarification. When you spoke of the role, Mr. Poplasen, the role of Mr. Karadzic in the Political Council, you said: "He would tell us that the party leadership had taken appropriate decisions." What did you understand to be the party leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the party Presidency and the Executive Board. That was the leadership which met frequently, as far as we know. The Serb Democratic Party was in power at the time and it had to take decisions within the state bodies. Now, when it comes to important matters, one knows that it is within the parties that discussions take place first, before the representatives in the government who are members of the party take further decisions. I understood these people to be party leadership members who were members of the state bodies which dealt with these matters, tried to avoid conflicts, tried to push for constitutional changes that would prevent the situation from deteriorating. One has to also take into account the fact that we expected that some sort of discussion was still taking place on the level of Yugoslavia and that we still hoped that Yugoslavia would continue existing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You wrote an article in 1991 in Oslobodjenje in which you set out your support for the idea of forming a People's Council as a second legislative house or body within the republic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This was a period of tension and intense efforts to find solutions. The way I saw it, the constitutional problem had to first be solved, and that's why I suggested that the People's Council be established as the second chamber in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where representatives of the three constituent nations would be equally represented; namely, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, and that within this council national interests would be preserved. And this was also the way, in my view, to avoid outvoting of one of two nations -- of one nation over two, and that was the best way to make compromises; to make an authoritative body that would continually point to the fact that bloodshed and war was the worst of all solutions to that problem. This article was published in the daily newspaper, which at the time had a very high circulation. It was subsequently upheld by many readers in their letters to the editor. As far as I remember, there was this letter, "The last call for help by a thirsty person in a desert." This was published by a person in Oslobodjenje who energetically supported my suggestion, and he was later an official of the Croatian Democratic Union in Bosnia-Herzegovina, however things turned out for the worse later on. Unfortunately, after the bloodshed and destruction that took place, the Dayton Accords saw that the right solution was in establishing the People's Council, and it was in fact established.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, first of all we are talking about an article, and of course if the Chamber could read that article, then we would become more familiar with the ideas of the witness. Sometimes I do not fully understand them. You said: Muslims, Serbs, and Croats would be equally represented in this council for the people, I think you said. And that would avoid outvoting. I still do not understand. I mean, if every nation would have one-third of the votes, still Muslims and Croats could outvote the Serbs, even in this new body. Or is this a wrong understanding? But that's of course -- I put the question not having any knowledge of this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd also like to read the article. We don't have it, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, all kinds of details as to whether the publisher was fully supporting the ideas, et cetera, of course seems to be of relatively minor relevance, so therefore -- but let's try to understand your testimony. How could, in this new body where there was equal representation, how could you avoid outvoting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to be brief, that is why I didn't go into detail. It was implied that there would be another chamber of representatives where decisions would be taken by a qualified majority -- simple majority, I suppose. In the Council of the Peoples, the decisions would be taken either by consensus or by simple majority of votes of every people separately. You are quite right: One of the provisions regulating the procedure of the Council of the People would be that the decision-making would be done through consensus or by a simple majority of votes taken from each of the peoples individually, not all of them together. That is why in this way outvoting would be prevented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let's just assume that the Muslims would by majority vote against a certain proposal, there would be no consensus, neither would there be a majority of votes of each of the peoples individually. So is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something of the sort is possible. It, in fact, happened, and that's why there was a war. We had outvoting, which is a fact. However, one presupposes that a debate by reasonable persons leads to reasonable arguments. The Council of the People would be able to re-introduce a certain matter on the agenda on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But from what I understand is that a system of being outvoted, which of course is very unpleasant if you are outvoted again and again, even if you have reasonable arguments, would be replaced by or supplemented by a system where one of the nations could just block any proposal by saying that no majority of this nation would support the idea, and therefore consensus was not there, neither was there a majority by all the three nations separately. I'm just trying to understand how it really resolved a problem which, from what I understood until now from the testimony, seemed to be very much a problem that could not or could not easily be resolved by this kind of structures but could, as you said before, perhaps only be resolved by everyone using common sense and not using majority positions or exploiting minority positions with a more or less effective veto.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you have just explained the situation as we are experiencing it currently in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is the constitutional situation in which we are now, where one people can block the other or any sort of solution. However, there is a specific situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina where we have an arbiter who is not from Bosnia-Herzegovina, if we can put it that way, who deblocks the -- such a stalemate. However, one can conclude that a High Representative would not be in Bosnia-Herzegovina for good and that representatives of the different people, if they want to live together, have to seek and find some legal mechanisms that would allow them to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say the situation has not really changed within Bosnia-Herzegovina, apart from someone now there to take decisions where decision-making is -- is not going as one would wish it to go. But the matter is clear to me. Mr. Josse, the Chamber would very much like to focus on these kind of analyses. If the witness says: Well, outvoting was a problem but we created the new body so as to avoid outvoting, whereas, at least for me, it was totally not understandable how outvoting could be avoided, and under the new system that I would say everyone is stuck in a similar situation, would be the same as in -- without this new body. These are the kind of dilemmas, I would say, the Chamber is very much interested in to hear about and not just to say: We had a new body and that would resolve the matters. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's a very helpful indication, Your Honour. My only observation is, as is clear, this gentleman has a great deal of detailed knowledge, notwithstanding -- bearing in mind his profession. And if one asks him questions like that, he's bound to take quite a long time in giving a full explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, unless you immediately interrupt and say: How could this new system avoid outvoting? If you would have stopped him there and immediately asked the question, then perhaps -- and perhaps guide him a bit in his answers to that, because as it appears now, outvoting was avoided but another mechanism which would obstruct decision-making in a sensible way as much as the outvoting system did would remain. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you a little about your own personal observation of tensions building up within Sarajevo. Did you see any visible signs that Muslims were taking up arms?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: The fact that the Muslims were arming themselves went around and it was much discussed. Later on it was confirmed by the Muslim side on the television and in the papers; however, one could also notice out in the street. From the start of the school year, that's to say in September and October of 1991, in the yard of the faculty of political science, where I worked as deputy dean, one could see uniformed persons walking by, and very often they carried weapons. There were members of the so-called Patriotic League. These were, therefore, not the police or any other regular law enforcement forces, but rather members of a force that had not been regulated by either the constitution or the law. Quite understandably, this contributed to instilling fear in people. And as you had occasion to see - this was recently published in the press - when you take a look at the provisions that were passed whereby double pensionable years of service were to be recognised for those who, as of April that year, participated in the arming process of the Muslim or Bosniak people in Bosnia. This evidently refers to those who contributed to the arming process and set up various units. This is now a piece of legislation which shows that this was indeed a fact. This could also be felt by the people in general out in the street. There were efforts to stop the situation from deteriorating, and this is in fact the topic that we have just discussed a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what year you meant when you are talking about April. Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to ask the same thing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said "as of April." April of what year? "... who, as of April that year, participated in the arming process ..." April of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The double pensions, Mr. Poplasen, is what the learned Judge is referring to.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: April 1991. This was the law on pensions or, rather, on social welfare in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the federation, that is. And I saw it published in a journal called Liljan. I believe the Defence has a copy of this information. They were quoting this provision, and it mentions the date and all the other details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I have a question. You said: "Later it was confirmed by the Muslim side on the televisions and the newspapers." Could you please clarify this: When you said "later," what does it mean "later"? And when was it confirmed by the Muslims? On what occasion? What did you mean exactly by this? Could you expound on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you what I mean by that. My memory is not so detailed, but more than once there were interviews on television with political and military leaders of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. For example, with Sefer Halilovic. In this interview he explained that the Muslim people, in the course of 1990 and 1991, armed themselves, that certain formations were established, they were expecting conflicts, and he spoke of his own significant contribution to this. And this is not an isolated example. There are many such interviews in the electronic media and in various publications which show the same kind of facts, and this is not difficult to establish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but those interviews, those publications, was it after the war, during the war, or right before the war? When exactly did that occur in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards the end of the war and after the war. These are people remembering these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would like, Mr. Poplasen, to move on, please, to April of 1992. There came a time when you had left Sarajevo for some sort of trip and you were physically unable to return because of a roadblock or some such-like problem. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I was unable to go back. You are right when you say that I was away on a trip, and on my return to Sarajevo there were barricades at the entrance to the town. And I was unable to pass through. The road was physically blocked. That was the morning of the 6th of April. From the Sokolac-Rogatica side in front of the tunnel called Kozja Cuprija, there was a roadblock. On one side of the tunnel were armed Serbs; on the other side were armed Muslims. Not only I, but nobody could pass through. The place was exposed to gun-fire, so I returned to Pale, which is not far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in Pale you got in touch with Professor Koljevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes. This went for a few days. I found accommodation in a building called Hotel Panorama, and two or three days later, because Pale is not a big place, it's a small town, I ran into some people in the street who were from the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party. They said that there were quite a few of them there and that they were staying in a hotel on the edge of Pale. I went there and there I met up with Professor Koljevic and some other people, and then things took a different course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think it might be helpful, Mr. Poplasen, if we -- or you summarised to the Chamber your activities in this part of 1992 and then we went back and looked at them again in a little bit more detail. Correct me if I'm wrong, but you basically worked alongside Professor Koljevic for approximately the next two months. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: A little less. What happened was the following. One should bear in mind that before the 6th of April, that is sometime in March, in the town of Sarajevo itself, not in Pale, after the misunderstanding in the National Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, an Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established and -- the elected MPs or its members. And they elected a government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This Assembly, in January 1991, adopted the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So there was already an Assembly, a government, there were certain documents, and the people who were members of the government and the members of the Assembly found themselves in Pale. And then they began to organise their political life, legal affairs, defence, and so on. I met up with Professor Koljevic, and I was engaged in looking for premises where these people could carry out their work and where work could begin on the -- on regulating the legal status of all this work and to organise contacts with the media. This was a lot of work, which is why I was in contact with Professor Koljevic. He was later in contact with President Karadzic and other members of the leadership of the Serb Democratic Party, whom I saw from time to time. But mostly I cooperated with Professor Koljevic on the issues I have mentioned. This went on for about two months, perhaps, until towards the end of May 1992, when I left that kind of work and went to a unit, and around the -- that was around the 20th of May. I went to a unit some 50 kilometres away from Sarajevo -- from Pale, which was commanded by a good friend of mine. Some days later, at the invitation of Professor Koljevic, I returned to Pale because he asked me to accept the role of republican commissioner in Vogosca municipality in order to regulate affairs in that municipality. I accepted his proposal. The Presidency issued this decision, and towards the end of June - I think it was the 28th of June, if my memory serves me well, I think it was the holiday of Vidovdan - I went to Vogosca as commissioner in that municipality. Occasionally I stayed in Vogosca. I didn't spend all my time there. One of the reasons for my dissatisfaction was my leaving Pale in -- that's why I went to the unit instead of working with the SDS. But in the meantime I clarified my political position and began establishing the Serb Radical Party of Republika Srpska. While I was in Vogosca as a republican commissioner, I had a car at my disposal, of course, which was owned by the Presidency of Republika Srpska. I used that car for party purposes. Very often -- I often toured all of Republika Srpska in the course of 1992, and in most municipalities I participated in the establishing of the steering committees of the Serb Radical Party, but this used up a lot of time, energy, and fuel. Of course I did not give up my role as commissioner in Vogosca, which I visited from time to time, because the commissioners I had -- which had been appointed were doing their job, and it was not up to us to hold power there but, rather, to see that the existing authorities were performing their duties in accordance with the law. This is very briefly a sketch of my activities after April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Breaking that down, you began by telling the Chamber that you were involved in logistical work in Pale. You did that in conjunction with Mr. Divcic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes. When wartime operations began, there was a place called Kikinda. It was a vacation hostel and it had been abandoned. There were problems with the utilities there and the furnishings and so on --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you because Mr. Divcic has told this Chamber about his activities there. It's right, isn't it, that he, as he in fact told the Chamber, concentrated on such logistical work, but you, in due course, started getting involved in more policy-orientated work in conjunction with Professor Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: That's correct. Several days after that - I can't recall the exact date now - President Karadzic arrived in Pale from Sarajevo. This was not on the 6th of April but a few days after that, about a week afterwards. Mr. Koljevic was there, and they had already agreed about the distribution of certain duties. And I accepted Professor Koljevic's suggestion that with him I should work on assessing international relations, contacts, and correspondence. In connection with this, I had daily meetings with Professor Koljevic where we discussed in great detail the positions taken by the United Nations, the European Community, the great powers, and so on, and discussing what our response should be. I assume that this had an influence on Professor Koljevic's letters and Professor Karadzic's letters, but I don't know how much of this is true because Professor Koljevic spoke English very well. He had a degree in English, and I did not look into his correspondence. But in any case my activities were focussed on that area. Up to a point, I was also active in organising the work of the Serbian radio and television station in Pale, but about a month and a half later, some problems emerged that had to do with humanitarian aid. This could not be monitored. There were technical problems. How to establish whether 20 trucks of humanitarian aid which had been sent had arrived at their destination. There was no method I could use to establish that. As the organs of the government had moved from Pale to Jahorina, it made work even more difficult because there were only a few telephone lines that could be used by the entire government there. I was not happy with this state of affairs, and so I informed the Prime Minister, and Professor Koljevic and I left to go to a unit. Maybe I was not being objective, maybe it was not possible to organise things otherwise, but it seemed to me that an extra effort should be invested because some things were beginning to happen - I won't say it was criminal activity - but things that it was difficult to monitor and track. So I left Pale to go to that unit, but then when they called me back, I returned, as I've already stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like you to deal briefly with the unit. The unit was where physically, please?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: It's north of Sarajevo. Its command post was some 10 kilometres away from the town of Olovo. Formerly it was in a village called Nisici, and the name of the unit was the Nisici Brigade. It was commanded by a civilian, Slavko Kojic, and I spent about a fortnight or 20 days there, helping him with advice in his command, advising him in his work, also talking to the civilian refugees, because a large number of Croats had fled through the territory of Nisici from Kiseljak and Visoko, and this unit was giving them logistical aid, food and so on, and directing them in the route they wanted to go. This unit was not at that time engaged in military conflicts. We were dealing with problems that were a consequence of the war: Feeding the population, dealing with refugees, finding accommodation for people, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For the avoidance of any doubt, did you join the army?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No. I joined the army only in 1994 when I was mobilised, as were other military-age men. I was mobilised into the student brigade in November 1994 as a university professor. Before that, I was working at the university.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we go any further, you told us that you had helped Mr. Koljevic when you were with him, that you also contributed to the work done by -- or for the radio and television in Pale. Could you be more explicit. Could you give us some details as to what your actual work was then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I was doing with Professor Koljevic, it was analysing, commenting, harmonising attitudes towards the position taken by the international factors, towards the Serbian people and Republika Srpska. At that time the European Community, the United Nations, and the great powers were putting forward various initiatives and various evaluations of the leadership of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for interrupting you. I did understand what your work was with Mr. Koljevic, but you also said that you participated in the work of the radio and television, or "I contributed," "I helped," and I want to know exactly what you were doing there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the point in time I mentioned, Serbian radio and television did not exist. We had to create the conditions for it to start operating. We had to find premises. We had to see whether it could be in the community club or somewhere else. We had to find people who had previously worked in Sarajevo in Bosnia and Herzegovina television and who had the necessary skills, who could see where equipment could be obtained. We also had to gather together some journalists. We had to get the Assembly organs to pass the necessary documents. All this was very time-consuming and exhausting, and if you don't have telephone lines, if transport is a problem, if you have to go around looking for a person who's supposed to be at his work-place but is not there for some reason, you use up a lot of time. When a man arrived in Pale, a literary man called Todor Dutina, who had experience with the media, he took over all this work. President Karadzic tasked him to take over this job as the director, and my obligations then ceased in that respect. Immediately after Mr. Dutina took this over - I can't recall the exact date - the first signal appeared. First SRNA began operating, the Serbian news agency, then Serbian radio-television, then Serbian radio began operating, obviously as a result of the hard work of Todor Dutina and his team. I made only the first few steps, which were technical and logistical, but the actual programme was something that was done by others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I was about to say given the long break I earlier requested, I've lost track and I'm entirely in Your Honours' hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we could have a break now or somewhere within the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This would be a convenient moment. We'll then have a break and re-start at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, how did you get to hear that you were going to be appointed a republican commissioner?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Well, yes, a commissioner, or an emissary you could say. But as far as I remember, one of the drivers or a courier reached Nisici, where I was staying, and informed me that Professor Koljevic had asked for me to come to Pale as soon as possible. I can't remember what date it was, but at any rate it must have been in the first half of June 1992. As I arrived in Pale, Professor Koljevic told me about the initiative he had launched and that he thought that a number of us were to assume the role. He said that in his opinion these were people who would be able to formulate the position of the state leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was renamed Republika Srpska. He also told me that this was a role entailing coordination and investigation as to whether the local authorities were acting within the constitutional purview and to point to any deficiencies in their work. This was necessary due to the fact that communication was very bad. Communication lines were severed between the government and the leadership of Republika Srpska and certain territories. Whenever the lines were functioning, it was impossible to present a political view in two minutes over the phone. That is why occasionally we had consultations with members of the Presidency and the government of Republika Srpska who were in charge of the work of commissioners. Following these consultations, we would each go back to the municipalities we were in charge of, take stock of the situation there, and report back to the government accordingly. The emphasis was placed on something that I and my party emphasised as important, which was the maintenance of the rule of law and the effort to constitute the state on legal bases. During any war, there are frequent instances of violations of laws, and there is also the possibility for chaos to reign. I saw this as one of the ways to prevent a chaotic situation and to constitute the state along certain legal principles, but also to solve some specific problems that the local authorities were unable to solve because of their very infrequent contacts with the state leadership. That is why I accepted Professor Koljevic's initiative and, as I've said, I received a written and signed decision to that effect by the Presidency of the republic where different commissions were listed and the roles of the commissions, as was the role of myself as a commissioner. I went to Vogosca and reported to the president of the Municipal Assembly and the president of the board.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There's a lot of information there, Mr. Poplasen. Again, you've dealt, in that long answer, with matters that I was going to turn to, so that's very helpful. But just before you deal specifically with going to Vogosca, I'd like you to have a look, please, at the minutes of the 5th Session of the Presidency, copies of which I have for all concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this, I am told, is part of P64, P65. The other copies were for the interpreters' booths, if it's thought necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We see at -- on this document that you were appointed a commissioner, along with five other people who are named in the document. Do you have any recollection whether you attended this session of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No. I don't remember that. I did not attend meetings of the republican Presidency. I don't recall being present; however, the minutes seem to be reliable and are consistent with my knowledge. All the more so because I was told the decision was taken on the 10th of June, and indeed all of these six persons listed here are familiar to me. I know them and they did assume their roles as commissioners, although on territories different than mine. And it's on that basis that I conclude that the minutes are reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't know whether I've got the exhibit number wrong. I see Mr. Harmon helpfully assisting on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's 529, tab 112.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have P64, P65, Treanor 12, tab 157.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I may have confused the minutes with the decision. So it's P64 Treanor, tab 17. In which binder, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's P64, and then it's P65, Treanor 12, tab 157.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next issue I'd like you to address is the term that was applied to the job that you were given. In the English translation that I have, it says: "A list was compiled of commissioners of the SBH state leadership, the following persons are appointed commissioners." On occasions we've heard the expression in English "war commissioners." Is there any difference? Are we talking about the same thing?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I think it's enough to say "commissioners," although war commissioners were dubbed that way because the word "war" denotes the time in which they were active. However, it's enough to say "commissioners." That's to say, the emphasis is placed on the fact that they are commissioners because they were not primarily concerned with war matters in terms of being military personnel. They did not have any powers over the army, and especially not in relation to war operations. It is true that this was a time of war throughout the territory, almost, but it would not be proper to tie these commissioners up primarily with war because their duties were of a -- of a civil nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
