utterances.text: You have already given us a description of the job and an explanation as to why you took the assignment. You were about to tell us about your going to Vogosca and how you put the job of a commissioner into effect in that municipality. Please do so now.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: To put it in several sentences, my duty was not to make any decisions or determine any measures, but simply to gain insight into the work of the local authorities. I made contact with the president of the Municipal Assembly and the president of the Executive Board. I informed them of the decision of the republican Presidency, which they accepted. They informed me of the state of affairs in the municipality where, at the time of my arrival there, there were occasional war conflicts along some of the lines. And they were periodical. One could not say that they were intense war operations or activities at the time that I arrived there; however, they had quite a few difficulties with their communication lines with the outside world. There was one part of territory that was under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When you went from Sarajevo towards Vogosca, there was the area around Olovo which was also under the control of the Army of BiH. And there was a lateral route across a mountain which was not easily trafficable. It was a dirt road. They had trouble bringing in supplies and had a dearth of food and medical supplies. They had difficulties in contacting whatever medical institutions were near when they had the wounded coming in, and we were discussing about the possible solutions. Another difficulty was that quite a few councilmen were either away travelling or were wounded, some had been killed, and the Municipal Assembly could not meet that often because they could not get in touch with them. However, the Executive Board met at least once a week in -- it met as a government, of course, but since there was a war on, it was also able to discharge some of the duties of the local parliament. I took stock of the situation and reported to Professor Koljevic, who was in charge of following the work of the commissioners. As I've said, I travelled quite often. I would go to Vogosca on some such matter. Since the commission itself was also set up, some of the persons who were quite active in Vogosca were deemed by me to be appropriate for that function. I provided Professor Koljevic with their names, and in my absence they were able to implement all the duties that were provided for the commission, and that's the way the work was done in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You observed a dispute of a trivial nature between the president of the Municipal Assembly in Vogosca and the president of the Executive Council, and presumably tried to resolve that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: That's correct. Between Mr. Stanic, who was president of the Municipal Assembly, and Mr. Koprivica. There was not -- you wouldn't be able to call it a conflict, but there was this friction which had to do with the work of the Municipal Assembly and the work of the Executive Board. Mr. Stanic wanted the Assembly to meet, but he simply could not be reasoned with. If he was unable to summon the minimum of deputies after having sent five invitations to them, then he had to simply come to terms with the fact that the Municipal Assembly cannot meet and that, in the absence of these sessions, the Executive Board could not simply -- not do anything. Mr. Stanic eventually came to terms with this and placed himself at the disposal of the work of the Executive Board and the local leadership, although it took several meetings between Mr. Koprivica and Mr. Stanic in order for them to understand that any conflict is only superfluous and that the matter had to be solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question. You said when Mr. Josse talked about the republican commissioner. You said: "Commissioner or emissary." What exactly did that mean for you? It seems that you made an analogy between those two words "commissioner" and "emissary." Could you please explain this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When one says "komesar" it reminds one of the communist times where a komesar had the duty to assess people in moral and political terms and to produce his own opinions about the person. So under the system where -- from which I come from, the term "komesar" "commissioner," has that connotation, whereas the other term in B/C/S "povjerenik," commissioner is a person who simply needs to accurately report on whatever he was tasked with to his superior body without changing the status quo in terms of legal regulations. This was our idea, that whatever could not be reported on in writing had to be reported on verbally. We -- our point of departure was that there were regulations governing the work of the local authorities, and we as commissioners were supposed to double-check whether the existing regulations were being consistently applied rather than introduce anything new. We had to double-check whether the local authorities acted in keeping with the regulations existing in Republika Srpska. If they are found not to do so, our duty was first to caution the local authorities about this and then the republican bodies, which were supposed to act on it from there. We did not have the authority to issue any orders. However, the local authorities were very well aware of the fact - at least, this was the way things were supposed to be - that after our intervention it was the Presidency or the government's turn to intervene. Our requests were logical and based on law, and it was a much better course of action for them to accept these comments of ours. The B/C/S term "komesar," to me, means something completely else, quite an arbitrary way of proceeding and looking for -- or rather, a fault-finding activity, rather than that which was issued to a "povjerenik."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you said there were very few lines of communication, just a few telephone lines. So those emissaries, wasn't it their job to circulate the instructions coming from central power? Since there were no lines of communication, wasn't that their job, the job of the emissary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was one of the tasks. If no other way was possible, then they would bring a piece of paper containing the given regulation or simply verbally inform them of regulations. There were people in the local authorities who were perhaps assigned to some other tasks, war assignments and so on and so forth. We as commissioners had that sole task, to report on the accurate situation from the ground to the republican level and then go back to the local level and inform them of the outcome of this consultation. In some instances the local authorities would not be aware of there having been a regulation passed. There was need to inform them thereof because in some cases the Official Gazette was unable to travel as fast to these areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but when you're answering my questioning, saying in English: "It was one of our tasks. If no other way was possible, then they would bring a piece of paper ..." and so on. Did it ever happen personally that you -- that you had to actually bring to Vogosca decisions or pieces of paper, as you say, on behalf of central power to Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know of such instances in some other municipalities. I personally did not have need to act that way, but I personally reported to the government and Presidency of Republika Srpska on the situation in Vogosca. As far as I knew, the Executive Board operated in satisfactory terms, given the general situation. That's why I did not have any need for any additional interventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to be so lengthy, Mr. Josse. There's a sentence that you said, in English, you said that: "The commission itself was -- the commission itself was set up and it was deemed for the function ..." and so on. Does that mean that on-site a commission was set up? What did you mean by that? You recommended people who were very active, as you say in English: "... deemed by me as appropriate for that function." What did you mean by that exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aside from me as the commissioner of the Presidency of Republika Srpska, a local commission was set up based on my proposal. There was me and there were four more people from the local community. I put their names on paper, and I sent the paper to Professor Koljevic, and these people were appointed municipal commissioners by Professor Koljevic on the basis of my initiative. They had the same role as the one described for a commissioner, which does not mean that they didn't have other duties within the Municipal Assembly or Executive Board. Whenever I went to Vogosca, these people would be there to inform me on whatever matter interested me. Interestingly enough, Vogosca is a municipality of Sarajevo and it was physically easier for them to reach Pale, where the Presidency was housed, unlike some commissioners that was a hundred kilometres away from Pale. This was also the reason why it did not take them as long to get hold of Official Gazettes with new regulations. In these other cases where the municipalities were further off, then the republican commissioner had to take a hard copy of these regulations with him and visit the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who were the four members of this commission? Not the names, but who were the -- their position? Who were those people? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the documentation I noticed that there was this decision with the names. These were people who lived and worked in the Vogosca area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was their position, their function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, I don't recall what their functions before the appointment as commissioners were; I only know that I wanted one of them to be a lawyer, the other one to be an economist, the other one -- the third one to have public relations experience. I wanted to have people from all walks of life so that I could rely on them and on the information they provide me with. I think that I've been more or less correct in naming their professions. I believe that they were within these same professions before they were appointed commissioners in their municipality and they were familiar with the people in the municipality. They knew the area. To me it was a totally new environment because I had not been to Vogosca before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're very clear: They had no real power except that they could control whether what the administration was doing was in accordance with the regulation. That's all they did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, but perhaps I should add that they also had to coordinate among them to see whether what was done was in accordance with the regulations and to coordinate between their level and the republican bodies, but they did not have any powers because they were not given any by the law. The regulations governing local authorities were a different matter, and they had to be abided by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few follow-up questions in this respect. Mr. Poplasen, you told us that you tried to find people from all kind of backgrounds. Was there any officer, military officer, in the war commission appointed in Vogosca, in the area where you worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was a colonel who was close to retirement age and who was not a brigade commander but had an unusual coordinating role, in my view. His role was to evaluate the military operations on that territory, and as I knew the man from before the war because he used to teach in the Department for National Defence at the faculty of political sciences, I put him in the committee to report to me on military affairs. The other members were not in the military, nor did they participate in the work. Colonel Vukovic's task was to evaluate the situation and report to me on the problems that arose. I was primarily interested in problems of logistics, health care in the military, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Was there any -- you emphasised that the commission was very much focussing on the legality of the local government. Did they in any way have any role in supporting the -- the military, or was it totally separate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military and military activities were a separate matter. What does "providing assistance to the military" mean? The members of the units in the area of Vogosca were mainly civilians who were mobilised locally and who belonged to those battalions and the Vogosca Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there any role for the war commissions in whatever relation with military matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps, if obtaining food and other material for the population and the military is part of military activity. The civilian authorities, including the commission, had to make sure there was no hunger in the area. One cannot say that food was not distributed to everyone, including members of the military. But the commission had nothing to do with issues such as fuel, ammunition, or weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was this a specific task to the commission or was it just your interpretation of -- that no one should suffer any hunger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone. Madam Usher, could you please assist the witness. There seems to be a problem with the -- is it plugged in properly, Madam Usher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my assessment, it was not humane to have someone go hungry if such a situation can be avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was not whether you would personally decide for someone to starve, but my question was whether this kind of support for the military was a specific task of the commission or that it was just your own interpretation of what was humane.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was not a specific task, for the commission to look after meals for the soldiers. We didn't even have any insight into their food situation. It was the general food situation in the municipality because communications had been cut off, as had supplies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the conditions of work for the military was not an official part of your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I look at the -- the decision of the 10th of June, decision of the same date by which you were appointed, and let me just read part of what war commissions should do, and I'm referring to P529, tab 112. It reads: "They shall cooperate with the authorities with a view to creating conditions for the work of military organs and units engaged in defending the Serbian people." That sounds a bit different from the answer you just gave. Could you assist me in reconciling them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They shall cooperate on creating the conditions. This can mean that a building has to be provided for the command, or perhaps an outpatients clinic, a field hospital --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me please -- I do understand. That's exactly why, when I put the question to you, I said: "So the conditions of work for the military was not an official part of your job?" Your answer was: "No, it wasn't." Now you start explaining what it was. Now you say they shall cooperate on creating the conditions, whereas in my earlier question I referred to those conditions and you said it was not an official part of the job. I mean, I do understand what creating conditions could mean; that it could be -- well, whatever, a building, food, a field hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand your additional question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you earlier answered to my question that there were in no way -- it was in no way part of the job -- let me just read it literally. I asked you: "So the conditions of work for the military was not an official part of your job?" And of course I was referring to your job as a state commissioner. Your answer was: "No, it wasn't." Now, being confronted with these lines of a decision by which war commissions are created, you start explaining how the commissions were part of the job by explaining that it could be providing for building or outpatients clinic, et cetera. So I have some difficulties in reconciling your earlier answer with the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In my submission, it would help if the witness could be shown the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, of course we could try to -- Mr. Usher -- Mr. Registrar, could you find P -- you might not have it here, but you can find it on -- perhaps print that out. It's P529, 112.1. It's a tif file which, if you move to your computer, Q drive, Exhibits, 112.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sorry, we are in the position to broadcast the B/C/S version on the screen, if that would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we could do that as well, but I see -- yes, and rightly, Mr. Registrar, you ignored whatever I said about the English version because it would not assist the witness very much, although he might read English. Witness, could you please - and that's what my question was about - read the last sentence of Article 3 of this decision of the 10th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The war commission shall cooperate with the organs of authority on creating conditions for the military organs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And last part of the sentence, "and ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's article 4. "And units in the defence of the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the units in the defence. So when I asked you whether the creation of conditions for the work or the conditions for the work of military organs were of any concern to the commissioners, you said, no, it was not, whereas from this part of this decision I understand that it was part of their official task, to cooperate in creation -- in the creation of such conditions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may make an observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my initial response I explained the answer to your question very well. When I speak of the conditions of work, what I mean is that the fighters and their family members should not go hungry. If the military command wants to move into a school, then a decision has to be issued. That means conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My next question then was whether this was an official task of such a commission or whether it was just your interpretation of humanity. You said it was not an official task. Then I asked: So the conditions were not of your concern, and then you said: No, they were not, whereas I now confront you with a document which says that this was an official task and not just consideration of humanitarian concern -- a personal consideration of humanitarian concern. But let's move on. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you want, Mr. Poplasen, to comment on the assertion the learned Judge has just made?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes. This interpretation of -- my interpretation of the word "humane" and the tasks here is a little exaggerated. Should people die of hunger or not. Eliminating hunger; is this something that is simply a humanitarian approach or is it implementation of Article 3? The essence of the problem was that the commission did not have any war tasks. But when war operations are underway, everything has to do with war. The music that is played on the radio can be linked up to the war because it creates a certain mood or a certain attitude. You can interpret this ad infinitum. It doesn't say here anywhere that the commission has any military tasks. If civilian authorities have to issue a document, handing over a school to the army rather than having the army take it by force, that's not what is meant by military tasks. And other regulations have to be passed. The army decides how long it will keep the building; that's how I understand conditions, not in any other way. When I said that we had no competences over the military, I was referring to planning, military operations, decisions as to who would participate in a military operation, when it would be carried out, by what means, supplies of weapons and ammunitions, command over the units, forming units, and so on and so forth. These are all military matters. I accept if a building, a premises, a food, health care, information, if these are considered to be conditions for military activity, then, yes, I accept this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, the matter is clear enough. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to help the Chamber with how often you were in Vogosca at the time you were a commissioner?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: One might say that I was not performing my duty properly because, as I explained, I was making use of the car and the fuel to tour the republic and set up branches of the Serb Radical Party. I would spend a few days in Vogosca, then be absent for a week or two or three, and this was observed by other people in the commission and the civilian leadership. Of course while I was there, if I noticed anything where I felt to intervene -- I had to intervene, I did intervene. But you could say that I was there quite rarely, not really often.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst you were there, did you observe at any time a place of either detention or collection of Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes. In the town of Vogosca, on the outskirts of the town, I went to have coffee and a brief conversation in a former restaurant or cafe called Sonja, or Sanja, or something like that. Mr. Vlace [phoen] was there; he was allegedly the warden. I parked the car in the parking lot in front of the establishment, and different people went in and out. I noticed Serb soldiers and people who might be described as prisoners or detainees, but they moved about quite freely. There was no armed guard in front of the building and there were no armed guards inside. The soldiers who were carrying weapons had them slung over their shoulders as part of their baggage. While I was having this conversation, I understood that there was certain people there who were occasionally sent to do work duty and that they were in some sort of transit. I don't know to where, but they were not obliged to stay in their rooms, they were not under very strict supervision, and they were able to move around to a certain extent. The problem of food was touched upon. I assumed that these were Muslims who wanted to leave Vogosca for one reason or another, and they happened to be there while waiting. I drew attention to the problem of food, and then we reached some decisions about supplies for the whole town, of finding new means to supply the town. This is what I observed. My impression was that this was some kind of detention centre or prison because people were collected there and they were under control, although not with weapons. So I wrote a letter to the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska in which I expressly asked that this institution, which I described in my letter, had to be either disbanded, or -- I don't remember exactly what I said but it must still exist somewhere, or that it should be integrated into the judicial system of Republika Srpska. My proposal was that this should be treated as part of a prison which existed from before in the Serbian part of Sarajevo, which had its regulations, its staff, its premises, and that it should be regulated in this manner. I think I sent a copy of this letter to Mr. Koljevic also. In any case, it was forwarded to the Ministry of Justice and, to the best of my knowledge, the Ministry of Justice responded to this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "responded to this fact"?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I mean that they issued the appropriate decisions; i.e., they integrated this -- these premises into the prison system of Republika Srpska, thereby including it in the system of rules and regulations. I was not able to follow this up in detail because it was already the summer of 1992, and the commission was abolished at the end of that year and I had nothing further to do with the organs of Republika Srpska; I was doing something quite different after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P379, which I know the registrar very helpfully has to hand. Probably best to put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is that the place -- my microphone is off? My microphone is permanently on, the red light is permanently on. That one doesn't work at all; the red light is not on at all. And on these two, the red light is on permanently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, use the one to the extent possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I can be heard, Your Honour, I'll go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no problems hearing you, but the interpreters need to hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Looking at the photograph, Mr. Poplasen, which is P379, is that the place that you are -- have just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No, no. The building I mentioned looked quite different; there was no fence around it either. And architecturally it didn't even resemble this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does that building remind you of anything, ring any bells, something you've seen before, anything that might assist the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: It doesn't remind me of anything. This is a typical building such as the buildings built by migrant workers who return from abroad and then build a huge house with ten rooms that they never use. Houses like that can be found everywhere, all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Since I've referred to that particular exhibit, Your Honour, I'll deal, if I may, with a topic slightly out of turn because I think it will make a little bit more sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so, but could we first -- let me just see whether I missed something. The name of the warden of the prison was -- I might have missed it. You may have said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The witness did say it, Your Honour, but in fact it was transcribed, understandably, wrongly. The name was Brano Vlaco, V-l-a-c-o, in Latin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does the name Ramiz Juzik [phoen] mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: No, I've never heard that name before. I don't know any person called that. I have never either met or heard of anyone with that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At any time in 1992, did you visit the Rajlovac barracks?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: I think I understand your question. In the course of 1992, I did not visit the Rajlovac barracks or any barracks. I did not enter any barracks, any place where soldiers sleep or are trained, either in Rajlovac or any other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's been alleged in this courtroom that you in common with -- along with Mirko Krajisnik and someone called Vlasto Apostolski visited those barracks on the 7th of August, 1992, and viewed a man who had been severely beaten. What do you say to that allegation?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: The name of Mirko Apostolski [as interpreted] doesn't mean anything to me. I don't know the person. As for Mr. Mirko Krajisnik, I met him later. I don't think it happened in 1992, but rather in 1993. And this meeting of ours was very brief and very fleeting. Somebody introduced him to me as Mirko Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is off again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it seems to be on again, but there seems to be some secret powers controlling our microphones at this moment. Mr. Josse, may I draw your attention to the fact that on the transcript it appears that in your question a Vlasto Apostolski was mentioned whereas the witness responded in relation to a Mirko Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's be clear about it: Does the name Vlasto Apostolski mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: Obviously I have to repeat this: The name of Vlatko [as interpreted] Apostolski doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. You told us about Mirko Krajisnik. Is there any truth in your visiting the Rajlovac barracks and viewing, sadistically almost, the man who'd been beaten?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: That's a complete fabrication. I didn't see the man, I didn't go to the barracks, I didn't know and I don't know the man Apostolski, whereas I met Mirko Krajisnik later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, if I may. The next issue I'd like you to address is one you have alluded to, and that is your decision to form the Serbian Radical Party. Why did you feel it was necessary to form that political party?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: The problem is how to answer your questions -- question in under 45 minutes. The first reason is that, in my opinion, pluralism was needed in Republika Srpska because the SDS rule, even though there was a war on, reminded me of the one-party system we had in the socialist system. The second reason is that my assessment was that in 1992 the Serbian issue was not resolved --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Again the microphone seems to be switching off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there is a technical problem with our microphones, because I can't switch mine off -- on. There seems to be a general problem in controlling microphones. I specifically ask the attention of the technicians for that. Let's try to see whether we can continue for the next ten minutes, but if it becomes hopeless -- I'll keep mine on, then that's the safest, from what I understand. Perhaps if we don't touch them, nothing will change. But first of all, we now should take care that the witness's microphone is functioning. Let me see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- I'm afraid that I was at the basis of it all, my block note being half on the priority button. I apologise, and I'll never take priority --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've succeeded in being shut out now, Your Honour, have I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Poplasen, you have given us the first reason for setting up your political party. So far as the second reason is concerned, you were saying that in 1992 the Serbian issue was not resolved. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA POPLASEN
utterances.text: In 1992, in my assessment, the circumstances in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Balkans, and in the area in general, the resolution of the Serbian national issue was going to take quite a long time, several decades, including all the other outstanding issues in the Balkans. That was why I was convinced that we have to have a very clear-cut orientation for the future. The policy had to be well-rounded and well-thought out because the next decade was the one where one could expect tensions, conflicts, and the expression of interests -- of some traditional interests of some of the countries around the Balkans, and I'm referring primarily to German and the Vatican. The third reason is one we already mentioned, which is that the SDS, which had formed legitimate government, having won the elections, had occasionally deviated from its policies. I think we've mentioned that already. The fourth reason was that, in my assessment, in this period of time the Serbian Radical Party in Yugoslavia, not to say in Serbia, was the party that best formulated the policy that I found acceptable, and that was the Serbian Radical Party with its leader, Vojislav Seselj. And lastly, the fifth reason was that, morally speaking, I could not accept leaving Republika Srpska by car or by bus and accepting some comfortable position as a lecturer somewhere, which was quite easily available to me. I was offered such a job in Belgrade. I simply could not agree to abandon my people and the community I lived in. When you look at all these reasons together, it was for these reasons that I worked in Republika Srpska to set up all the different branch offices in the lead-up to the inaugural session of the party. In early 1993, I had already taken up employment with the faculty in Banja Luka, and on the 20th of March, 1993, the inaugural session of the Assembly of the Serbian Radical Party was held. At this inaugural session, where I was elected president of the party, some of the names of the commissioners we saw on the list there, one of them was vice-president of the party and another one was general secretary of the party. In addition to the jobs we had, like my employment with the faculty, we intensely worked on the political platform of our party. As an opposition party, we were also in a position to criticise the Serbian Democratic Party. Quite often, we exaggerated in our criticism for propaganda reasons. Already in 1994, we assessed that we were quite highly rated as a party by the population of Republika Srpska, and we started insisting the general elections being called. This was one of the reasons why, although on quite a rarely -- rare basis, I demanded that I meet with the -- Mr. Krajisnik, who was speaker of the Assembly, as president of my party. And on several occasions, I also asked to meet with President Karadzic, although, admittedly, I went to see him as part of a delegation of the Serbian Radical Party as a whole. The leadership of the Serbian Radical Party, which had already become a parliamentary party in Serbia - I'm referring to the one led by Vojislav Seselj - this party would come to visit Republika Srpska, and I would be part of that delegation because I was at the same time vice-president of the whole party. It is true that our head office was in Belgrade, and this was called the central party administration for all the offices. And I was vice-president of this central party, of which Mr. Vojislav Seselj was president, and at the same time I was president of the Serbian Radical Party of Republika Srpska. There was this legal play, we could call it that. Since we had accepted the legitimacy of Serbian Democratic Party, which had in turn apparently accepted the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, maybe not in a decision but through it's conduct, we registered the party in Republika Srpska, that's why it's called the Serbian Radical Party of Republika Srpska, and formally speaking, it was independent. Formally speaking, I did not have any ties with the Serbian Radical Party and Vojislav Seselj. However, we had this central administration, central homeland administration, of which I was a member. So formally we were only linked to this administration because had we been established as a party from a different country, we would not have been able to take part in the elections. That is why we formally registered there. And we exerted pressure for the general elections to be called. President Karadzic had quite a few harsh statements leveled against our party, maybe it was motivated by the fact that our party was quite popular. At any rate, in this dynamics, our party grew and the elections kept being postponed. In our constant press releases, we criticised steps taken by the Serbian Democratic Party. And one of the targets of our criticism was the Socialist Party and President Milosevic. The crucial parts of our criticism are explained in -- can be deduced from my numerous statements and books which I wrote and which contain some of my public statements from the period, that's to say between 1992 and 1995. There are several books dealing with these events alone. There were three key issues why we criticised the Serbian Democratic Party and Belgrade, and so on and so forth. I already mentioned one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there because in fact that was my very next question. I was going to ask you what your dispute was with the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I see the time and I'll resume tomorrow with that question, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may. We'll first ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom, but before doing so, Mr. Poplasen, I would like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now and you're still about to give tomorrow. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Poplasen out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back, Mr. Poplasen, tomorrow morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Afternoon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- afternoon at quarter past 2.00. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, could you give us an estimate on how much time you'd still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm bound to be another session, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm glad Your Honour's raised the issue in the absence of the witness. I was in two minds whether I should, because of course I'm aware that the Defence don't have any other witnesses in The Hague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- and the Court is going to need to make a decision about Friday. But I suspect the decision is made, based on what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that many of the answers very often go with some detail into areas which seems not always to be relevant. Of course, it's difficult for me to forecast at this moment how important any conflict with other parties was, because it's not the position of the party of the witness that is the core of what we would like to hear about, but of course we can never exclude that from this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It appears what the other parties --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just tell the Court what my thinking is on that? I would imagine the Prosecution are bound to ask the witness what he thought was wrong with the SDS, for I'm anxious to deal with it first. He's going to cross-examine after. It's, in my submission, a fairly core issue and this witness is well-known as a fierce critic, on occasions, of the SDS, and a critic of what they did in 1992. Therefore, in my submission, it's pretty pertinent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- without knowing the type of criticism, it's of course difficult for this Chamber to form any opinion about it, and the Chamber of course does not want to form any opinion about it before we have heard the testimony of the witness. But you are the one who would know best how relevant it is. I noticed that very often the witness goes on and goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then I hesitate to stop him and ask you whether these were exactly the issues you would like to have raised in your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not really, although the only thing I would say, particularly about this witness, is he does tend to cover matters which I would have had to come to in due course. So very little of what he says is superfluous in the submission that I make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's try to see how we can deal with the -- his examination as efficiently as possible tomorrow. Mr. Harmon, may I take it, although I'm aware of the unpleasant situation the Prosecution finds itself in in this respect, that you could cross-examine the witness tomorrow once Mr. Josse has finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will be in a position to start our cross-examination, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Then we will adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
